Rockstar’s “final big score” before GTA VI is a mass economy nerf disguised as a museum heist.

And I actually bought GTA+ for this update.
Seriously? This is what I paid for?

The Kortz Center Heist should have been a celebration of GTA Online after nearly thirteen years. Instead, Rockstar used it as an excuse to make some of the game’s most popular money-making activities significantly worse, seemingly so this overpriced new heist would look generous by comparison.

To host the Kortz Center Heist at full price, a new player needs a Mansion starting at GTA$11.5 million and the mandatory Art Studio expansion costing another GTA$4.7 million.
That is GTA$16.2 million just for permission to host the content.

Even when discounted, the Art Studio is still millions for what is essentially another planning room. The Kosatka costs GTA$2.2 million and unlocks Cayo Perico. Here, Rockstar expects players to own one of the most expensive properties in the game and then purchase a separate GTA$4.7 million room inside it.

After paying that absurd entry fee, you do not receive a streamlined or uniquely ambitious heist. You get a scope-out mission, six mandatory preparation missions, five optional preparations and another finale built around driving across the same twelve-year-old map collecting equipment.
That would be acceptable if the robbery remained properly rewarding.
It does not.

Your first Primary Target sale of the week can produce a decent solo total of around GTA$2 million once secondary loot is included. Repeat the exact same content during that weekly period and the Primary Target can fall to roughly GTA$400,000.

The Mansion does not become cheaper.
The Art Studio does not become cheaper.
The preparation workload does not shrink.
The travel time does not disappear.

Rockstar simply declares that the same kind of stolen painting is suddenly worth a fraction of its previous value because you already played the new content once that week.
They describe this as “market saturation” and “buyer fatigue.”
I describe it as turning a replayable heist into a glorified weekly login task.

You can technically play it solo, but your limited carrying capacity means you cannot get anywhere near the full gallery take. Crew members also have very little reason to help when their rewards can be pathetic compared with the host’s first weekly payout. After everyone completes their own weekly sale, the incentive to continue playing falls apart.

The finale is not polished enough to excuse this economy either. Players are already reporting inconsistent lasers, awkward detection, broken preparation missions, loading issues and Quick Restart leaving the finale in an alerted state after stealth is lost. Instead of restarting cleanly, you can be forced to abandon the finale entirely just to make another proper stealth attempt.

Even Michael’s heavily anticipated involvement barely amounts to anything meaningful. After years of players requesting his return, Rockstar once again uses recognition and nostalgia to advertise content without delivering the substantial story appearance people expected.

But the Kortz Center’s own problems are only half of why this update deserves a negative review.

Rockstar simultaneously changed payouts throughout GTA Online.
They call the new system a “weekly completion bonus,” but what that actually means is that the normal repeatable payouts have been lowered. You receive an increased amount once each week, then reduced earnings if the host repeats that activity before the weekly reset.

Here are the actual changes.

Cayo Perico has been nerfed again:
Sinsimito Tequila fell from GTA$630,000 to GTA$400,000 — a 36.5% reduction.
The Ruby Necklace fell from GTA$700,000 to GTA$560,000 — a 20% reduction.
Bearer Bonds fell from GTA$770,000 to GTA$616,000 — a 20% reduction.
The Pink Diamond fell from GTA$1.3 million to GTA$910,000 — a 30% reduction.
Cayo’s secondary targets were also reduced by roughly 10%. Cash, artwork, weed, cocaine and gold are all worth less than they were before this update. The target rotation now follows a weekly system too, with an 80% chance of receiving Tequila if you repeat Cayo during the same week.
The Diamond Casino Heist received a flat 30% repeat-payout reduction across its major targets:
Normal cash fell from GTA$2,115,000 to GTA$1,480,500.
Normal artwork fell from GTA$2,350,000 to GTA$1,645,000.
Normal gold fell from GTA$2,585,000 to GTA$1,809,500.
Normal diamonds fell from GTA$3,290,000 to GTA$2,303,000.
The Doomsday Heist was hit even harder, with normal repeat payouts reduced by 40%:
Act I fell from GTA$975,000 to GTA$585,000.
Act II fell from GTA$1,425,000 to GTA$855,000.
Act III fell from GTA$1,800,000 to GTA$1,080,000.
The Dr. Dre Contract finale fell from GTA$1 million to GTA$900,000 on repeat completions.
Cluckin’ Bell fell from GTA$500,000 to GTA$400,000.
KnoWay Out fell from GTA$350,000 to GTA$245,000.
The so-called weekly bonuses do not even restore Doomsday to its previous payout. The first weekly normal completion now pays GTA$714,870 for Act I, GTA$1,044,810 for Act II and GTA$1,319,760 for Act III — all still substantially below their old values.
Doomsday was already one of the longest, most difficult and least efficient ways to earn money in GTA Online. Nerfing it by 40% is completely indefensible.

The original five heist finales were also moved into this weekly completion system, alongside Casino, Doomsday, Cluckin’ Bell, the Dre Contract and other activities. Rockstar did increase payments for Original Heist and Doomsday setup missions, and some activities receive a worthwhile first-weekly bonus, but that does not justify cutting the repeatable finales people bought entire properties to access.

Players paid millions for Arcades, Facilities, Agencies, Kosatkas and other businesses because those properties unlocked reliable content. Rockstar has now retroactively weakened that content and attached weekly restrictions to more of the game.

They did not make the Kortz Center competitive by designing a better heist.
They made the competition worse.

That is the entire problem with modern GTA Online. Instead of respecting the player’s time, Rockstar manufactures inconvenience. Every property costs millions. Every new car costs several million. Useful features are divided between separate businesses and upgrades. Progress is deliberately slowed, and conveniently, Rockstar continues selling Shark Cards while offering a paid GTA+ subscription on top.

Really, I got GTA+ for this?
A temporary discount on an absurdly priced Art Studio, one early vehicle and the privilege of watching Rockstar nerf content I already owned? What a waste.

With GTA VI approaching, Rockstar should be increasing payouts, removing outdated restrictions and letting players enjoy GTA Online’s enormous backlog. This should be the period where the economy is opened up and the community is rewarded for supporting the game for more than a decade. Instead, they appear determined to squeeze the final Shark Card purchases and GTA+ subscriptions they can get before players move on.

The museum itself looks good. The concept of stealing real paintings, replacing them with replicas and displaying stolen artwork inside your Mansion is genuinely cool. There are pieces of a good update here but unfortunately, those ideas are buried beneath a GTA$16.2 million full-price entry requirement, eleven possible preparation missions, heavily reduced repeat payouts, more Cayo nerfs, enormous reductions to Casino and Doomsday, weekly restrictions, bugs and another layer of aggressive monetisation.

At this point, Rockstar is doing more to push PC players back toward GTA V Legacy and FiveM than toward the official GTA Online experience.

So for this remaster you get:
[list]
[*]Capped at 120FPS now, game used to run unlocked on PC but not anymore as of this new release. The game for some reason also defaults to half refresh rate VSync and still offers refresh rate options despite the framerate being locked now.
[*]No more text chat in GTA Online.
[*]Frame Generation only in a future update (Ah yes, the "release now, patch later" mindset).
[*]No DualShock 4 support, despite supporting DualSense controllers.
[*]No HDR display support on PC, while the console versions have it.
[*]Some people are reporting stuttering issues.

Now onto the raytracing that this version of the game has, it's fairly subtle, but in the cases that you do notice it, there's some issues:
[list]
[*]Mirrors in apartments (Franklin's room comes straight to mind), car mirrors, and such aren't using raytraced reflections.
[*]Raytraced reflections have really odd looking blurry cubemaps and other visual artifacts from a distance even with the highest settings (why this game doesn't offer a future-proofing setting to try and minimize this further is beyond me).

The game does run better than the original version, and the visual enhancements are nice, but it's not a night-and-day change. Despite what you'd expect, the Ray Tracing implementation is probably one of the least-intensive new features, and yet seems to be exceedingly good in that it demonstrates an understanding that it is best used sparingly for a gentle injection of realism rather than absolute perfect mathematical duplication of light ray pathing that tanks any but the most expensive computers. Reflections look nicer, shadows in the world feel more realistic, reflected light from coloured surfaces colours other surfaces...they've used the technology to add little touches of flavour, which makes it run much better than it otherwise might. The overall effect is, in my opinion, better than Ray Tracing in games like Cyberpunk because the small touches offer noticeable but realistically subtle improvements to the world without having to show themselves off, while decent performance allows it to be accessible to most players. 

That said, it's still  the same game - a spacious, but vacuous and utterly misguided affair. The rose-tinted glasses most certainly come off after your first playthrough, let alone 12 years after release. The missions vary wildly in quality, but are largely a boring, linear slog. You will spend far too much time all throughout the game observing the rubber-banding of the vehicle you're supposed to be chasing as the game urges you to 'catch this person', when it knows full well that you'll only catch them at the exact scripted moment. Races are always rigged to be too easy because they're not that interesting, and you'd be hard-pressed to want to repeat them if they were harder. The world is intensely detailed on a macro level, and a cardboard cutout on the player-level. The shop directly across from Franklin's house is a good example of a movie-set facade that you're supposed to drive by and not notice, yet it's placed directly in front of one of your most visited locations. It  feels like you should be able to enter it, and yet it's one layer away from being a single 'store interior' texture slapped on the outside wall and stands out like a sore thumb. On every level, attempts to interact with the massive map are as fulfilling as staring at a concrete wall with a pretty field painted on it and trying to smell the flowers. There are next to no activities to do of any real worth beyond the main missions - you can go to a car wash, or sit and watch cutscenes of your character talking to a therapist, or invite a 'friend' to ride a ferris wheel. You can go to the cinema and watch a bunch of short films that are all produced with the same 'subtle as a sledgehammer' tone as the gratingly unfunny radio ads. None of these activities are entertaining or impactful to your experience, and the more fidelity Rockstar gives its worlds, the more lazy and facilie its satire appears, and the more starkly its lack of interactivity stands out. 

The distance makes driving from one location to another a chore, and venturing to the entire other side of the world only offers more mechanically tedious minigames, plastic pedestrians, buildings you can't go into, and police that will track your exact location right up until the allotted amount of time in hiding has passed. The main characters are all unrelatable and unlikable. Michael is a clueless, angry loser. Franklin whines relentlessly about every single person he knows. Trevor is, now more than ever, an absolute mistake as a protagonist - a punishment for players who do the things the game encourages them to do, disguised as self-awareness. Like all GTA V's attempts at saying something meaningful, Trevor's playability, and most missions in which you take control of him make the game less fun at the same time as they fail in their superficial messaging. If he were a mirror for the player then you might be inclined to reflect on your behaviour and not be like him, but you can't not be like him because you *are* him. Not one character in the game offers any hope for personal growth or has any meaningful goals other than 'get money'. Every single side character is an irredeemable annoyance. The sole concept is that America - and LA specifically - are sh*tholes that turn their inhabitants into miserable creatures. But I wonder if, at any point, the Housers considered that playing as miserable people whose only aspiration was to sit higher up on the pile of turds might not be very fun or interesting? Switching between three characters makes it feel like you're constantly being forced away from whichever one you can tolerate the most to fart about as someone else until the game offers you nothing else to do unless you switch characters again. And eventually the story ends and you're left stuck in the box with a bunch of cash and nothing to do with it, because without the main missions the world of GTA V becomes completely inert.

GTA V is, in my opinion, the most fundamentally flawed and empty of all the mainline games. I'd argue that it has the least interest in allowing players to indulge the location, with GTA IV being a close second, but this game's story is less focused, less compelling, and the characters you play as aren't really worth rooting for. It made a huge splash because it was a new GTA (at the time), it was a next gen GTA (at the time), and it was viewed as a technical achievement (at the time) because of its size and scale, before everyone clued into the fact that bigger worlds are actually boring as hell and a smaller, more condensed environment with a distilled personality and more interactivity was a far more enjoyable experience. I went to Grove Street and found a note in Ryder's back yard - 1 of 50. How in the hell am I supposed to locate 49 other needles in an 80sq/km haystack? Why would I care to? 

Lastly, I suppose the Online portion of the game was a fun novelty for a while before it became a Horseman of the Apocalypse for depraved, exploitative monetisation. This novel gamemode is now generally regarded as a slop trough casino for the publisher as they wring the most vulnerable, addictable personalities amongst their player base dry, pouring cash better spent elsewhere into the slavering maws of corporate executive hogs that use that exact revenue stream as an excuse to not create new stories. It's pathetic.

If you already own the game, then this review means nothing. Is it worth a buy in 2025 for someone who hasn't yet played it? Nah. GTA IV is a better story with better characters in a world relatively on-par in terms of how interesting it can be. RDR2 is a better world with more interactivity.
